HAV-019.transcript:
Cleared out the storeroom for the water-tank guys and found Dad's box. The five-page police file. His phone, dead -- I charged it. His little pocket diary, the one he wrote petrol receipts in. I sat on the floor and read all of it.

And here's the thing. The report says he was alone on the rock. But the forest gate register is stapled at the back, and it has a scooter going in at five past six -- fifteen minutes before Dad's car -- and coming out at 7:35, "fast," the guard wrote. And nobody in the report ever mentions that scooter again. Why did that never come up?

I'm probably being stupid. It's been six years. I'm probably being stupid.

HAV-021.transcript:
I made a timeline. Dad's car in at the forest gate at 6:20, that's in the register. The scooter in at 6:05, before him. A jogger told the police she heard two men arguing up at the rock at about ten past seven, and one of them said "stay away from her." That's a direct quote, it's in her statement. The report puts the fall at "about 7:15." Alone.

Then Dad's phone. The last call in was 5:48 that morning, from a contact he'd saved as "R (Meera's friend)." The police wrote one line: "family friend, informed." Informed. They called him to TELL him Dad was dead, and never asked why he'd phoned Dad at ten to six on a Sunday.

The report says one thing, and the register and the jogger and the phone say something completely different, and the file just... moves on. I can't stop thinking about this. I emailed N. about it because he's the only person I can say this to who won't tell me I'm grieving weird.

HAV-022.transcript:
I went to Turahalli today. First time since. The gate guard from 2018 is still there, older, same chair. He remembers the young man on the scooter. Rucksack, glasses, said he was going to meet a family friend up the trail. The guard told the police all of that. Nobody ever came back to ask him anything.

And there's the effects list. Wallet, phone, keys, water bottle, and a blue carabiner with a little club tag, "TD 2018." Dad didn't own a carabiner. Dad didn't own anything with a tag on it. Someone was up on that rock with him. Someone dropped that.

I haven't told Arjun any of this. I don't know how to start.

HAV-025.transcript:
Someone emailed me. Last night, quarter to midnight. No name. An address that's just numbers. It said, "Whatever you think you're looking into, stop. This is the only warning you'll get."

I have read it maybe forty times. Who has this email? I only use this address for -- for a handful of people. Someone knows I'm investigating Dad's case. Not "someone might know." Someone knows.

I locked the balcony door twice and then checked it again. Bruno keeps looking at the door.

HAV-027.transcript:
I think I'm being watched. I don't say that lightly.

The gate guard -- I went back to thank him -- said someone had already been by asking what I'd wanted. This week. Somebody knew I went to the forest, and I told exactly no one.

Then Rahul called tonight, out of nowhere, just to chat, asked what I've been up to. And I said "nothing." Why did I say nothing? He's the one person I could always tell everything. I think I'm just scared of everyone now. That's what this is doing to me.

HAV-028.transcript:
Another email. "I know where you've been going. I know who you've been talking to." They know about the forest. They know about the gate guard. They might know about N.

I drafted a leave request for next week so I can go to the district office in person, first thing, before anyone can pull anything else out of that file.

Arjun and I had a real fight tonight, a bad one, and it was about nothing, and it was about everything, and I couldn't tell him the actual reason I've been like this. I wanted to. I got as far as "there's something about Dad" and then I just... didn't.

HAV-029.transcript:
I'm close. I can feel it.

The jogger. I found her -- she's "S. Iyer" in the statement, she still runs there. She remembers more than the statement says. A young voice, and an older one, and the older one said, loudly, "I told you to stay away from her." Her. Dad said "her." And then a bit later a young man came running down the trail past her with no rucksack and blood on his knuckles, and she thought he'd fallen.

And then there's Dad's little pocket diary. Same year, three separate pages, the same note: "Talked to R. again. Warned him off." And a note on his phone from the Saturday night, the last thing he ever typed: "Sun. Talk to R at the rock. End it."

I've been staring at that R for an hour. I don't want to say the name. I'm not going to say the name until I'm sure, because once I say it I can't unsay it.

HAV-030.transcript:
Rahul messaged tonight. About passwords, of all things -- "you still use that?" -- and then, out of nowhere, about the cave. Whether I remembered our kingdom. Whether I still cheated at hide-and-seek.

It was sweet. It should have been sweet. Instead I sat here afterwards with Dad's diary open in my lap, looking at one letter, and I felt sick.

I'm going through his Loop in the morning. Every trek photo. Then I'll know. I need to know before I say anything to anyone.
